title: Cozy Bedtime Stories for Adults 🌙 Candlelight, Pumpkins and Late Radio | Snortlo
intro: Hello, and welcome. This is Snortlo, and tonight I have six gentle stories for you, about candlelight, late night radio, a garden full of pumpkins, and a few other quiet places. Before we begin, let yourself get comfortable. Dim the lights, or switch them off. Let the pillow hold your head, and let your hands go loose. You don't need to stay awake until the end. If you drift off halfway through a story, that is exactly right. Take one slow breath in, and let it out even slower. Let's begin.

stories.title: The Overnight Show
stories.text:
At the top of a narrow building on Harbour Street, above a bakery and a shop that sold buttons, there was a little room with one window and one microphone. Every night at midnight, a man named Walt climbed the stairs to that room, switched on the red lamp by the door, and said good evening to whoever might be listening.

The station was small. It reached the town, and the farms on the hill, and a few boats out in the bay if the weather was kind. Walt had hosted the overnight show for nineteen years. He liked the hours. He liked the way the town went quiet beneath him, one window at a time, until only the streetlights and the lighthouse were left awake with him.

He kept a thermos of tea on the desk, and a tin of shortbread, and a notebook where he wrote down the requests. There were not many requests. There were three listeners he could count on, and he thought of them as his regulars.

The first was Mrs. Lowe, who ran the bakery downstairs. She started work at three in the morning, mixing dough while the ovens warmed, and she liked something with a piano in it. She would phone the station at a quarter past three, every night, and say the same thing. Good morning, Walt. Something with a piano, please. Then she would hang up before he could answer, because her hands were already floury.

The second was a farmer named Henry, who lived on the hill and got up early to see to his cows. Henry never asked for a song. He only asked for the weather, and he asked for it in great detail. Walt suspected Henry knew the weather better than anyone, and only wanted to hear it said out loud by someone else, the way you might want to hear your own name.

The third was a lighthouse keeper named June. She didn't phone. Instead, at around two in the morning, she would flash the lighthouse lamp twice, a little faster than usual, and Walt would see it from his window. That meant she was listening, and that she was fine, and that he could play whatever he liked.

Tonight it was raining, a soft and steady rain that made the window shine. Walt settled into his chair, put on his headphones, and leaned toward the microphone.

Good evening, he said. It's just past midnight, and it's raining on Harbour Street. If you're awake, I'm glad of the company. If you're falling asleep, I'm glad of that too.

He played a slow song, something with a cello in it, and poured his first cup of tea. Steam curled up past the red lamp. Down below, a cat walked along the wet pavement, stopped under a streetlight, and looked up at his window as if it had heard him.

At one o'clock, he read the weather. Rain until morning, he said, easing off around dawn. Light wind from the west. The sea is calm in the bay. Temperatures falling slowly, so if you're going out early, take a scarf. He said it carefully, with a little pause between each part, because he knew Henry would be listening on the hill with his boots by the door.

At two o'clock, he looked out of the window. Far off, past the rooftops, the lighthouse turned its long slow beam across the water. Then it flashed twice, quick, quick. Walt smiled.

Good evening, June, he said into the microphone, though he never said her name on the air. Instead he said, This next one goes out to everyone keeping watch tonight. And he played something gentle, with a guitar and the sound of the sea in the background.

He ate a piece of shortbread. He read a letter someone had mailed to the station, from a child who wanted to know if the radio man ever slept. Walt read it out loud, and answered it. I do sleep, he said, I sleep all morning, with the curtains closed and a very warm blanket, and I dream about tea.

At a quarter past three, the phone rang. Walt picked it up.

Good morning, Walt, said Mrs. Lowe. Something with a piano, please. Then the click.

He found a record with a piano on it, a slow one that sounded like rain falling on a tin roof. He let it play from start to finish without saying a word. Downstairs, he could almost smell the dough rising. He imagined Mrs. Lowe humming along as she shaped the loaves, dusting the counter with flour, sliding the first trays into the warm ovens.

The rain eased a little after four. The streets were shining and empty. A delivery van went by slowly, its wipers going back and forth, back and forth, and then the street was quiet again.

At five, Walt read the weather once more. The rain is stopping, he said. The clouds are thinning out over the hill. It will be a clear, cool morning, and the sun should be up a little after seven. He paused. Henry, he thought, would be pulling on his boots now, and opening the barn door, and saying good morning to the cows.

Then he read the tide times, because someone always wanted them, and he played one last song. He picked a quiet one, with a soft voice humming along, nothing hurried, nothing loud.

When it finished, he leaned in close to the microphone.

That's the overnight show, he said. Thank you for staying up with me. If you're just waking, there's fresh bread downstairs, and the rain has stopped. If you're still trying to sleep, close your eyes. There's nothing else you need to do tonight.

He switched off the red lamp. He rinsed his cup, and packed his notebook into his bag, and put the lid back on the shortbread tin.

Downstairs, the bakery window glowed yellow. Mrs. Lowe waved at him through the glass and held up a warm roll. He went in, and she gave it to him wrapped in paper, and neither of them said very much. They didn't need to.

Walt walked home slowly as the sky turned pale. Behind him, out over the bay, the lighthouse turned once more, and then, as the morning came in, it rested.

stories.title: The Pumpkin Count
stories.text:
On the edge of a small town, past the last house on Mill Road, there was a long, low field divided into garden plots. Each plot had a little shed, or a bench, or a scarecrow made out of an old coat. Some plots grew beans, and some grew flowers, and one grew nothing but enormous cabbages. But the plot at the very end, by the hedge, belonged to a man named Theo, and Theo grew pumpkins.

Every year, on the first cold morning of autumn, Theo came down to his plot before anyone else was awake, and he counted them.

He woke early that morning, while the house was still dark. He could feel the cold before he opened his eyes. It was in the tip of his nose and the edge of his ear, and he smiled under the blanket, because he knew what kind of morning it was. He got up quietly, so as not to wake his dog, who was very old and liked to sleep in. He made a flask of hot tea with milk and honey. He put on his thick wool jumper and his good boots, and his hat with the flaps that came down over his ears.

Then he walked down Mill Road in the half light. The houses were dark. A few chimneys had a thin line of smoke going up, straight as a pencil, because there was no wind at all. The grass on the verges was white with frost, and it crunched softly under his boots. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

At the gate to the gardens, he stopped and looked. The whole field was silver. Every leaf, every fence post, every bench had a fine white coat of frost on it. The cabbages looked like they had been dusted with sugar. The scarecrow in the old coat had frost on his hat brim, like a little white moustache.

Theo walked along the grass path to the end, past the beans and the flowers and the cabbages, until he came to his own plot by the hedge.

There they were.

The pumpkins sat among their big, tired leaves like a family of round, orange people having a rest. Some were huge, and some were small, and some were a funny shape, a little flat on one side from leaning against their neighbours all summer. The frost had settled on their tops, and as the sky got lighter, they began to glow.

Theo unscrewed his flask and poured a cup of tea. He held it in both hands for a moment, just for the warmth. Then he took out a stub of pencil and a little notebook, and he began to count.

One, he said, touching the first pumpkin gently on its cold, ridged side. That was the big one near the gate. He had watched it grow all summer, from a little yellow flower to a green ball to this round, heavy, glowing thing. Two, he said, and three. Those two were twins, almost the same size, sitting side by side. Four was a small one, hiding under a leaf. He had to lift the leaf to find it, and when he did, a little brown bird hopped out from underneath and gave him a cross look before flying off to the hedge.

Sorry, said Theo. I didn't know you were staying there.

Five, six, seven. Seven was a pale one, almost white, which he had grown from seeds a neighbour had given him. Eight was very long, more like a sleeping cat than a pumpkin. Nine was the smallest of all. It would fit in his two hands. He thought it might be his favourite.

He kept going, slowly, down the rows. The sky behind the hedge turned pink, and then gold. The frost on the field began to sparkle. Somewhere in the town, a church bell rang seven times, slow and far away.

When he had finished, he wrote the number in his notebook. Twenty three. He looked back through the pages at the numbers from other years. Nineteen. Twenty one. Seventeen, the year it rained all summer. Twenty three was the best he'd ever had. He wrote it again, a little larger, and drew a small circle around it.

By now, other gardeners were arriving. There was Ruth, who grew the flowers, carrying a basket and wearing two scarves. There was Mr. Pell, who grew the cabbages, and who never said much, but always nodded. They saw Theo standing in his pumpkin patch with his notebook, and they knew what day it was.

How many, called Ruth.

Twenty three, said Theo.

Ruth clapped her gloved hands together. Mr. Pell nodded twice, which was a great deal, for Mr. Pell.

Theo poured them each a little tea in the lid of his flask, and they stood together by the hedge, sipping and watching the sun come up over the field. The frost was beginning to melt now. Little drops of water ran down the sides of the pumpkins and made them shine.

Over the next week, Theo would carry the pumpkins up Mill Road in his wheelbarrow, two or three at a time. He would leave them on doorsteps around the town. One for the woman who walked his dog when his knees were sore. One for the little school on the corner. One for the bakery, who would turn it into soup. The very big one would go to the town hall, where children would sit beside it and have their pictures drawn. And the smallest one, the one that fit in his hands, would sit on his own kitchen windowsill until the spring.

But that was for later. For now, the sun was warm on his face. The tea was sweet. The field was turning from silver to green, and twenty three orange pumpkins sat glowing in the morning light.

Theo screwed the lid back on his flask. He tucked his notebook into his pocket. He walked home slowly up Mill Road, past the chimneys and the quiet houses.

At home, his old dog was still asleep on the rug, exactly where he had left her. Theo sat down in his chair by the window, still in his jumper and his hat. He thought he would close his eyes, just for a minute. Outside, the last of the frost slipped quietly off the roof.

stories.title: The Candle Maker's Last Batch
stories.text:
At the bottom of a cobbled lane, in a town where the streets were too narrow for cars, there was a small shop with a green door and a window full of candles. The candles were every shape and colour you could think of. Tall thin ones like reeds. Short round ones like little moons. Candles in tea cups, candles in jam jars, candles shaped like pears. The shop belonged to a woman named Mabel, and every evening after she closed, she made one last batch.

She turned the sign on the door around, so it said closed, and she pulled down the blind. The lane outside was dark and wet, and the street lamp at the corner made a soft orange circle on the cobbles. Inside, the shop smelled of a hundred things at once, honey and pine and oranges and woodsmoke, all mixed together into something warm.

Mabel tied on her apron. It was an old canvas apron, covered with drips of wax in every colour, like a painting nobody had meant to make. She went into the little workroom at the back, where there was a big copper pot on a low stove, a long wooden table, and shelves full of glass bottles with handwritten labels.

She lit the stove. The flame was small and blue. She put the blocks of pale wax into the pot, and while they slowly began to soften, she went to the shelves to choose tonight's scents.

Mabel named all her candles after seasons. Not just spring and summer and autumn and winter, but the small seasons in between, the ones that only last a few days. She had one called First Frost, which smelled of cold air and peppermint. She had one called Puddle Season, which smelled of wet earth and green leaves. She had one called The Week Before the Holidays, which smelled of cinnamon and oranges and a hint of something like brown paper.

Tonight she wanted to make a new one. She stood in front of the shelves for a long time, reading the labels, lifting the little bottles one by one and smelling them with her eyes closed.

Outside, it began to rain properly. She could hear it on the skylight, a soft drumming, pat, pat, pat, and the gurgle of the drain pipe by the back door.

The wax was melting now. It went from white and cloudy to clear and golden, like warm honey. Mabel stirred it slowly with a long wooden spoon. Round and round, round and round. She liked this part. It could not be hurried. If you rushed the wax, the candles came out bumpy and cracked. If you were patient, they came out smooth as river stones.

While she stirred, she thought about the season she wanted to capture. It was the one that happens in late autumn, on the first evening you need to light the fire. The evening when you come home a little cold, and your fingers are stiff, and you kneel in front of the fireplace with a match. The first wisp of smoke, the crackle of the kindling catching. The smell of the wool blanket you have just taken out of the cupboard, after a whole summer folded away.

She took down a bottle of cedar wood, and a bottle of vanilla, and a tiny bottle of smoke that she used only a drop at a time. She took down one more, which smelled of clean wool, and another of baked apples, just a little. She mixed them in a small glass dish, a few drops each, and held it to her nose.

It wasn't quite right. It needed something softer. She added a drop of honey. She smelled it again, and smiled. There it was. It smelled like a warm room on a cold night. It smelled like the first fire.

She took the pot off the heat and let it cool for a little while, just until it was the right warmth. She stirred in the scent, and the whole workroom filled with it. The rain kept pattering on the skylight.

Then she set out the jars. She had twelve of them tonight, small and squat, made of thick glass with a little greenish tint. In each one she placed a wick, standing straight up in the middle, held in place with a wooden peg laid across the top. She checked each one, nudging the wicks so they stood perfectly upright.

Mabel lifted the pot carefully with both hands and began to pour. The warm wax flowed out in a slow golden ribbon. She filled the first jar almost to the top, and moved to the next, and the next. She did not spill a drop. She had done this ten thousand times, and her hands knew the way.

When all twelve were filled, she stepped back and looked at them in a row on the long table. They glowed softly under the lamp, like twelve little ponds of honey. As she watched, the edges began to turn pale and cloudy, as the wax started to set.

Now she needed a name.

She sat down on her stool, with a cup of tea that had gone a little cold, and she thought. She could call it First Fire. That was nice, but it didn't feel finished. She could call it Blanket Night. That made her smile. She could call it The Evening You Come Home Cold.

In the end she cut twelve little paper labels and wrote on each one, in her neat, slanted writing, The First Night by the Fire. She would tie them on with string in the morning, when the candles had set.

She washed the copper pot, and wiped the long table, and put the bottles back on their shelves in their proper order. She hung her apron on its hook. The rain had slowed to a gentle patter.

Before she turned out the lamp, Mabel took one candle from a shelf in the shop, one she had made the year before, called Late Autumn Rain. She lit it, and set it on the windowsill of the little room upstairs where she lived.

Then she climbed into bed, under a heavy quilt, and watched the small flame for a while as it flickered and settled. The rain whispered on the roof. The whole house smelled of cedar and honey and woodsmoke.

Her eyes grew heavy. She leaned over, and with one soft breath, she blew the candle out. A thin ribbon of smoke curled up into the dark, and the room was warm, and still, and quiet.

stories.title: The Last Note at the Bandstand
stories.text:
In the middle of the town park, where the paths all met, there was an old bandstand. It was round, with a pointed roof like a hat, and painted white, with little iron railings all the way around. In summer, a band played there every Sunday evening, and people brought blankets and sat on the grass to listen. But tonight was the last concert of the year, and when it was over, it was a man named Walter Bell who stayed behind to stack the chairs.

The concert had ended just as the sun went down. The band had played a slow waltz to finish, and then a march, and then, because everyone clapped so long, one more slow waltz. Then the musicians packed their instruments into their cases, said goodnight, and walked off along the paths with their coats over their arms. The families folded their blankets. The children were carried home asleep on their parents' shoulders. And then the park was quiet, and the only people left were Walter and a small brown dog who belonged to nobody in particular, but who came to every concert.

Walter had been stacking the chairs for twenty years. He liked doing it. There were forty folding chairs, all made of wood, with green paint that had worn away at the corners where people's hands held them. He walked from row to row, folding each chair with a soft clack, and carrying them two at a time to the little storeroom under the bandstand steps.

Clack. Clack. The little dog followed him from row to row, as if supervising.

The evening was cool. It was the first evening that really felt like autumn. The leaves on the tall trees around the park had turned yellow and red, and when the breeze moved through them, a few drifted down and landed on the grass. One landed on the seat of a chair just as Walter was about to fold it. He picked it up, looked at it, and put it carefully in his coat pocket.

The lamps along the paths came on, one after another, glowing softly through the branches. Out on the pond, the ducks were settling in for the night under the willow tree, making small, sleepy sounds to each other.

When all the chairs were folded and stacked, Walter went up the steps onto the bandstand itself. The music stands were still there, in a half circle. He folded those too, one by one, and laid them in a wooden crate. He swept the floor with a broom, gathering up a few leaves, a sweet wrapper, and a single sheet of music that someone had dropped. He looked at it. It was the slow waltz. He smoothed it flat and put it in the crate, so whoever had lost it would find it next year.

Then there was only one thing left on the bandstand. In the middle, under a canvas cover, sat the old upright piano.

The piano had been there longer than Walter. It had been painted white once, to match the bandstand, but the paint had faded to the colour of milky tea. Some of its keys were a little yellow, and one of them, a high one near the end, didn't play at all. Every year, at the end of the last concert, Walter wheeled the piano into the storeroom, where it would sleep through the winter under its cover, wrapped in an old quilt.

But before he did, he always played one note.

He wasn't a musician. He could not play a song, not even a simple one. But many years ago, when he first took the job, he had sat down at this piano at the end of the season and pressed one key, gently, just to hear what it sounded like in the empty park. And the note had floated out over the grass and the pond and the trees, and he had thought it was the loveliest sound he had ever heard. So he had done it every year since.

Walter pulled back the canvas cover and folded it neatly. He lifted the lid over the keys. The little dog sat down on the top step and looked at him, its head tilted to one side.

Walter sat down on the piano stool. He looked at the keys for a while. He always took his time choosing. Some years he picked a low note, deep and round, that seemed to go down into the ground. Some years he picked a high note, bright and thin, that seemed to go up into the stars.

Tonight he chose one right in the middle. Not too high, not too low. A warm, ordinary note.

He pressed it gently and held it down.

The note floated out from under the pointed roof. It drifted across the grass, past the stacked chairs and the lamp posts. It went over the pond, where one of the ducks lifted its head to listen. It went up through the yellow leaves of the tall trees and out into the dark blue sky, where the first stars were coming out. It got softer, and softer, and softer, until Walter couldn't tell if he was still hearing it, or only remembering it.

He let go of the key.

The park was very quiet. A leaf came down and landed on the piano lid. The little dog lay down on the top step with a long, contented sigh.

Walter closed the piano lid. He put the canvas cover back on and tied its strings. Then he wheeled the piano slowly down the ramp and into the storeroom, and wrapped it in the old quilt, tucking it in at the corners, the way you would tuck in a child. Goodnight, he said quietly. See you in the spring.

He locked the storeroom door. He took one last look at the bandstand, standing white and empty under the lamps, its pointed roof against the stars.

Then he walked home along the path, with his hands in his pockets, and the yellow leaf still tucked inside one of them. The little dog walked beside him as far as the gate, then turned and trotted off toward wherever it slept.

When Walter got home, he put the leaf on his kitchen table, next to nineteen others, each one from a different year. He made a cup of cocoa. He sat by the window.

And somewhere in the back of his mind, very softly, the warm middle note was still playing.

stories.title: The Cobbler's Notes
stories.text:
On a quiet street called Elm Lane, between a bookshop and a shop that sold teapots, there was a cobbler's shop so small you could touch both walls if you stretched out your arms. Over the door hung a wooden boot, painted red, swinging gently in the wind. Inside worked an old man named Mr. Pell, who had been mending shoes for most of his life.

Mr. Pell's shop smelled of leather and polish and the little paraffin heater he kept under his workbench. The walls were lined with shelves, and the shelves were full of shoes waiting to be mended, or waiting to be collected. There were work boots with worn heels, and dancing shoes with loose straps, and children's sandals with broken buckles. Every pair had a brown paper ticket tied to it with string, and on each ticket, in pencil, was a name.

It was a grey afternoon in late autumn. The rain had stopped, but the street was still wet, and the sky was the colour of a pigeon's wing. Mr. Pell sat at his bench under the window, with his glasses on the end of his nose, and worked.

He was mending a pair of brown leather boots that belonged to a postwoman named Nora. She walked many miles every day, and the heels had worn right down on the outside edge, the way they do when someone walks the same path a thousand times. Mr. Pell prised off the old heels with a small flat tool. He cut new ones from a thick piece of leather, tracing the shape with a sharp knife, slowly, slowly, following the line. He fixed them on with tiny nails. Tap, tap, tap. Tap, tap, tap. His little hammer made a soft, even sound, like a clock that had decided to tick very gently.

When the heels were on, he trimmed the edges smooth with a file. Then he took a soft cloth and a tin of brown polish and worked the polish into the leather in small circles. Round and round, round and round. The boots began to shine like conkers.

When they were finished, Mr. Pell did what he always did. He took a little square of paper from a drawer, and his pencil, and wrote a note. He thought for a moment first, looking at the boots, the way they had worn, the long miles they had carried someone.

Then he wrote, These have walked a very long way for you. The new heels will take you a long way more. Mind the puddles on Elm Lane.

He folded the note and tucked it inside the left boot. Then he tied on the ticket that said Nora, and placed the boots on the shelf by the door, ready to be collected.

Mr. Pell had been leaving notes in shoes for nearly forty years. He couldn't remember exactly when he had started. It might have been the day a little boy came in with a pair of shoes so worn the toes were open, and looked so worried that Mr. Pell had wanted to send him something cheerful along with the repair. Whatever the reason, he had never stopped. Some people kept the notes. Some people wrote back. There was a whole tin of replies on the top shelf, letters and drawings and thank you cards, and on slow days Mr. Pell took it down and read them again.

Next on the bench was a pair of small red shoes with a broken strap. The ticket said June, and underneath, in different handwriting, someone had added, she is five. Mr. Pell held them up to the light. The strap had snapped clean through. The soles were scuffed at the toes, the way shoes get when someone runs everywhere and stops by dragging their feet.

He cut a new strap from soft red leather, as close a match as he could find. He stitched it on with strong thread, pushing the needle through, pulling it tight, pushing it through again. He added a new silver buckle, shiny and small. Then he polished the toes until the scuffs were almost gone.

For June's note, he wrote, These shoes are very fast. Please be careful not to run faster than them. And he drew a small picture of a red shoe with tiny wings on the heel.

Outside, the street lamps came on. The window of the teapot shop next door glowed yellow. A man walked past with an umbrella he didn't need anymore, swinging it like a walking stick.

The last pair of the day was a pair of old black dancing shoes, the kind with a small heel and a strap across the top. The ticket said Ruth. Mr. Pell knew Ruth. She was eighty one, and she went dancing every Saturday night at the hall by the river. The soles had worn so thin he could almost see light through them.

He took his time with these. He lifted off the old soles, gently, so as not to stretch the soft leather above. He cut new soles of thin suede, the kind that let a dancer turn smoothly on a wooden floor. He stitched them on by hand, with small neat stitches all the way around. It took nearly an hour, and he didn't mind at all. He hummed a little while he worked, an old waltz he remembered from somewhere.

When he finished, he set the shoes on the bench and looked at them. They looked ready to dance.

He thought about Ruth's note for a long time. Then he wrote, Saturday night is waiting for you. Save me a waltz. And he smiled to himself, because he knew she would.

He tucked the note into the right shoe, tied on the ticket, and put them on the shelf next to June's red shoes and Nora's brown boots.

Then he tidied his bench. He put his little hammer back in its place, and his knives in their leather roll, and the tins of polish in a neat line. He swept the leather shavings into a pile and brushed them into the bin. He turned off the paraffin heater, which ticked softly as it cooled.

He put on his coat and his cap. He switched off the lamp over the bench. In the dark, the shoes on the shelves were just shapes, rows and rows of them, waiting patiently for their owners, each one with a little paper ticket and a name.

Mr. Pell stepped outside and locked the door. Above him, the wooden red boot swung gently in the wind, creak, creak, creak.

He walked home along Elm Lane, his own old shoes making a soft and steady sound on the wet pavement. They were the oldest shoes he owned, and the most comfortable, and he had mended them himself more times than he could count.

And tucked inside the left one, where only he knew it was, there was a little folded note that said, Well done today. Time to rest.

stories.title: The Last Post Before the Holiday
stories.text:
In a small town by the sea, on the corner of the high street, there was a post office with a blue door and a big round clock above the counter. It was the last evening before the winter holiday, and the post office had closed at six. But inside, the lights were still on, because there was one more job to do.

The postmistress was a woman named Ruth Lowe, and she had worked there for thirty years. Every year, on the last evening before the holiday, she stayed late to sort the final post. Every letter and card and parcel that had come in that day would be sorted into its proper place, so that in the morning, the post van could take it all out to the town and the farms and the little villages along the coast.

Ruth made herself a pot of tea in the little kitchen at the back. She put two biscuits on a saucer. She took off her cardigan and rolled up her sleeves. Then she went out to the sorting room, where the post was waiting.

There was a lot of it. There were three big canvas sacks of letters and cards, slumped against the wall like tired dogs. There was a trolley stacked with parcels of every size, wrapped in brown paper and string, or in bright paper with stars on it, or in old cereal boxes taped up very carefully. And there was the sorting frame, a tall wooden cabinet against the back wall, with rows and rows of little wooden slots, each one labelled with the name of a street, or a farm, or a village.

Ruth loved the sorting frame. It was older than she was. The wood had gone dark and smooth with years of hands reaching into it. The labels on the slots were written in ink, in many different handwritings, from all the postmasters and postmistresses who had worked there before her. Harbour Street. Mill Road. Elm Lane. The Old Rectory. Top Farm. Bottom Farm. Lighthouse Cottage.

She opened the first sack and lifted out a bundle of cards. She sat on her tall stool in front of the frame, and she began.

The first card was for Elm Lane. Into the slot it went, with a soft whisper. The next was for Harbour Street. The next was for the Old Rectory. Ruth's hands moved quickly, almost by themselves. She had done this so many times that she hardly needed to read the addresses anymore. She knew most of the handwriting. She knew that the shaky blue writing was from the old man on the hill, who wrote to his sister every week. She knew that the card with the drawing of a reindeer on the envelope was from the twins at number nine, sending a card to their grandmother.

Whisper, whisper, whisper. The cards slid into their slots.

Outside, it had begun to snow. Ruth could see it through the frosted window, small soft flakes drifting down past the street lamp, settling on the roofs and the windowsills and the little red post box on the corner. The high street was empty. All the shops had closed. A few windows above them were lit, warm and yellow, and in one of them she could see a small tree with coloured lights.

She finished the first sack, and opened the second. She drank a little of her tea. It was still warm.

In the second sack, she found a letter addressed in a child's handwriting, in big wobbly capitals, though Ruth read them as gentle letters in her head. It said, to the lighthouse keeper, the lighthouse, by the sea. There was no proper address. There was no street name. But Ruth knew exactly where it was going. She smiled and slipped it into the slot for Lighthouse Cottage.

There was a card with no stamp, which she stamped herself from the little drawer under the counter, because it was the holidays, and because the card was for a woman who lived alone at the end of Mill Road. There was a parcel that rattled, and a parcel that smelled of oranges, and a parcel that was very light and very soft and almost certainly a knitted scarf.

The clock above the counter ticked. Tick. Tick. Tick. Eight o'clock. Nine o'clock.

Ruth finished the second sack, and then the third. By then, every slot in the sorting frame was full. Some were so full that the cards stuck out at the top like feathers. She stood back and looked at it, the whole town's worth of good wishes, all sorted into their places, all waiting.

Then she started on the parcels. She checked each label and wrote a little number on the corner in pencil, so the driver would know which round it belonged to. She stacked them in the big wire cages by the back door, the large ones at the bottom and the small ones on top, so nothing would be squashed.

The very last parcel on the trolley was small and square, wrapped in brown paper, tied with red wool instead of string. Ruth turned it over to read the label. Then she stopped, and read it again.

It was addressed to her. To Ruth, at the post office, on the corner of the high street.

She looked at it for a long moment. Then she untied the red wool and opened it.

Inside, there was a small tin. And inside the tin, there were biscuits, homemade, shaped like little envelopes, with a tiny stamp drawn on each one in pink icing. There was a card, too. It was signed by what seemed like half the town. The twins at number nine. The old man on the hill. The lighthouse keeper. The woman at the end of Mill Road. There were dozens of names, all squeezed together in different colours of ink.

It said, Thank you for always getting it there.

Ruth sat down on her tall stool. She didn't say anything. She just held the card for a while, and listened to the clock ticking, and watched the snow falling past the window.

Then she ate one of the envelope biscuits. It was very good.

She put the lid back on the tin and tucked the card into her bag. She switched off the light over the sorting frame, and the light over the counter, until only the small lamp by the door was left. The sorting frame stood in the dark, full of cards. The wire cages stood by the back door, full of parcels. In the morning, the van would come, and all of it would go out through the snow, to every street and farm and cottage.

Ruth put on her coat and her scarf. She turned off the last lamp. She stepped out into the snow and locked the blue door behind her.

The high street was white and quiet. Her footprints were the only ones. She walked home slowly, past the red post box with its little cap of snow, past the window with the small coloured tree.

At home, she put the tin on the kitchen table, and the card on the mantelpiece, where she could see it from her chair. She sat down, and wrapped a blanket around her knees, and watched the snow.

And in the post office on the corner, in the dark, the big round clock kept ticking, soft and slow, all through the quiet night.

outro: And that is the end of tonight's stories. The radio show has signed off, and the bakery window glows. The pumpkins sit warm in the morning sun. The candles are setting in their jars, and the old piano is tucked in for the winter. The shoes wait on their shelves with their little notes, and the post office clock ticks on through the snow. There are more stories like these on the channel, whenever you need them. Goodnight, and sleep well.
